name: Ipeka-Tapuia
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Glottolog lists no descriptive refs; retired ISO code, dialect/clan of Curripaco [kpc] - check Curripaco sources instead

new_statements.quote: O acento recai, mais frequentemente, na penúltima sílaba, havendo também considerável número de exemplos de palavras com acento na antepenúltima e outros na sílaba que antecede a antepenúltima. Todavia, como mencionamos na introdução deste tópico, o acento não atua somente no nível silábico, mas no moraico também, assim no caso das sílabas longas tônicas, há ainda um segundo acento que recai sobre a mora, fazendo que haja sílabas tônicas de tom descendente e as sílabas tônicas de tom ascendente. [p. 189:] [...] as evidências indicam que se trate, portanto, de pitch accent o tipo do padrão acentual em Baniwa do Içana e em Kuripako.
new_statements.translation: Stress falls most frequently on the penultimate syllable, there being also a considerable number of examples of words with stress on the antepenultimate, and others on the syllable preceding the antepenultimate. However, as we mentioned in the introduction to this topic, stress does not operate only at the syllable level but at the moraic level too; thus in the case of stressed long syllables there is a further, second accent that falls on the mora, so that there are stressed syllables with falling tone and stressed syllables with rising tone. [p. 189:] ... the evidence thus indicates that the type of accentual pattern in Baniwa do Içana and in Kuripako is pitch accent.
new_statements.citation: de Souza, Erick Marcelo Lima. 2012. Estudo fonológico da língua Baniwa-Kuripako. MA thesis, Universidade Estadual de Campinas (Unicamp).
new_statements.locator: Sec. 4.6.2 'Acento e duração', printed pp. 188-189 (pp. 188-189; lines 8540-8551 and 8590-8592)

new_statements.rule_in_words: One prominent (pitch-accented) syllable per phonological word, never the final syllable; most often the penultimate, but frequently the antepenultimate or earlier, so surface position is not predictable from syllable count. On accented long syllables a lexical rising-vs-falling melody is superimposed. Ramirez 2001 (Central dialect only) derives the same distribution from a penultimate rule plus lexically extrametrical suffixes; Ortiz Ovalle 1998 (Colombian Kurripako) calls the accent free with a first-syllable tendency and preference for heavy syllables; Valadares 1994 (Kumandaminánai = Ipeka clan; second-hand via de Souza p. 41) found a paroxytone accentual culmination.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary word stress is described. de Souza's 'segundo acento' is the moraic rising/falling contrast inside the single accented long syllable, not a second stressed syllable. Ramirez 2001 explicitly limits his account to primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 190: nouns whose first syllable has a long stressed vowel lose both stress and length when a possessive prefix is added, stress moving rightward (['he.ma] 'anta' vs [no.he.'ma.ni] 'minha anta'); p. 191: the author hedges that more data are needed to settle pitch accent vs tone. Ortiz Ovalle 1998: stress can fall on any syllable (minimal pairs). Ramirez 2001 (Central): most onomatopoeias unstressed; suffix metricity is lexical.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including possessive prefix + noun); elicited citation forms. de Souza states the rule jointly for Baniwa do Içana (Hohodene speakers) and Kuripako; his Kuripako consultants are from Jerusalém on the upper Içana, one Kapitti Minanai (basis of the Kuripako analysis) and one Payualíene with a Kumada-Minanai mother (pp. 66-67) - the Payualiene/Cumata clans that Ethnologue 15 listed under Ipeka-Tapuia. Examples in (119) are given 'dos dois dialetos'. No phrase-level rules in any source.
new_statements.identity_note: ipek1240 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO code paj, merged into Curripaco [kpc] = curr1243 on 2008-01-14 (ISO CR 2007-004: 'Ipeka-Tapuia [paj] is a dialect / clan of Curripaco [kpc]'). Ethnologue 15's alternate names (Cumata, Ipeca, Pacu, Paku-Tapuya, Payualiene) identify it with the Kumada-Minanai and Payualiene clans of the upper Içana/Aiari; Koch-Grünberg (via Ortiz Ovalle 1998 p. 63) gives Ipéka-Tapuyo = Kumáta-Mínanei, Rio Aiari; Ramirez 2001 p. 39 and de Souza 2012 p. 51 place Kumada Minanai and Payualíene in the Northern superdialect 'dito curripaco/Kuripako'. No source describes a variety under the name Ipeka-Tapuia; the quoted statement is de Souza 2012's joint Baniwa-Kuripako statement, whose Kuripako data include a Payualíene/Kumada-Minanai speaker. The same statement is already recorded under curr1243 (pending verification). by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) a retired code does not make a separate language, so this should fold into curr1243 rather than become a separate catalog entry.

new_statements.quote: Kurripako follows the general syllable structure, (C1) V {(V) (C2)}. As is common in many Arawak languages, C2 is restricted to only nasals and is generally the result of vowel elision, most commonly /i/. [...] The phoneme /h/ generally occurs word initially, aspirated segments are at morpheme boundaries. Kurripako has pitch stress (or pitch accent) that interacts with vowel length. [p. 75] // [fn. 11, p. 51:] Vowel length will not be included because length and stress are related and since the data does not have the stress information marked in the transcription, it would not have been appropriate to deal with one without the other.

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record exists (in_catalog false). Agrees in TYPE with the existing statement (de Souza 2012: accent is a pitch accent, most often penultimate) — Granadillo also calls it pitch stress / pitch accent tied to vowel length — but gives no placement, so it neither confirms nor disputes the penult tendency. Variety differs: the sketch is of the Ehe-Khenim dialect of Venezuelan Kurripako; the Içana Ipeka / Kumada-Minanai / Payualiene clans appear only in clan-name and classification lists (pp. 47, 57-59), not as the object of description.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kurripako (Ehe-Khenim dialect, Venezuela) is characterised as having 'pitch stress (or pitch accent)' that interacts with vowel length; vowel fusion is described as an interaction of stress and length, and every grammatical word has at least two moras. No statement of where the accent falls; stress is not marked in the author's transcriptions (fn. 11).
new_statements.exceptions: none; no placement rule is given at all
new_statements.identity_note: Granadillo 2006 describes the Ehe-Khenim dialect of Kurripako as spoken in Venezuela (data also from Aha/Kurri), not the Ipeka-Tapuia (Kumada-Minanai 'Duck-people' / Payualiene 'Pacu-people') clans of the upper Içana/Aiari in Brazil that the retired code paj denotes; both fall under Glottolog curr1243 after the ISO 2007-004 merger of paj into kpc.

sources.citation: Granadillo, Tania. 2006. An ethnographic account of language documentation among the Kurripako of Venezuela. PhD diss., University of Arizona. 235 pp.
sources.quote: Kurripako follows the general syllable structure, (C1) V {(V) (C2)}. As is common in many Arawak languages, C2 is restricted to only nasals and is generally the result of vowel elision, most commonly /i/. [...] The phoneme /h/ generally occurs word initially, aspirated segments are at morpheme boundaries. Kurripako has pitch stress (or pitch accent) that interacts with vowel length. [p. 75] // [fn. 11, p. 51:] Vowel length will not be included because length and stress are related and since the data does not have the stress information marked in the transcription, it would not have been appropriate to deal with one without the other.
sources.locator: Sec. 3.7 'Grammatical sketch of Kurripako, Ehe-Khenim dialect', 3.7.1 'Phonology', printed p. 75 (the text); footnote 11, printed p. 51 (the text)
sources.note: Grammar sketch of Venezuelan Kurripako (Ehe dialect) with a phonology chapter; the SAPHON inventory built from it records no suprasegmentals, so it may state that stress is non-contrastive or describe it - needs checking; not the Ipeka clans.

sources.citation: Ramirez, Henri. 2001. Línguas Arawak da Amazônia Setentrional: comparação e descrição. Manaus: EDUA. Ch. 2 Baniwa-Curripaco; sec. 2.1.5 'Acentuação', pp. 88-96; dialect table p. 39.
sources.harvard_location: Tozzer Library (offsite storage), call number PM5476 .R36 2001
sources.note: p. 88: 'Limitaremo-nos ao dialeto central e ao acento primário'; rule box p. 89 and p. 46 point 10: the pitch accent never falls on the last phonetic syllable and always on the syllable immediately preceding the last metrical syllable (lexically extrametrical suffixes), i.e. penultimate by default; lexical rising/falling melody on long vowels, so 'pitch accent' not tonal (p. 94). Stated for the Central dialect (Huhúdeeni etc. = bani1255) only; p. 39 places Kumada-Mínanai (= Ipeka) in the Northern superdialect 'dito curripaco'.

sources.citation: Ortiz Ovalle, Maribel. 1998. Introducción a la lengua kurripako. Forma y Función 11: 55-75. Sec. 3.4 'Unidad prosódica: el acento', p. 71.
sources.note: p. 71: 'El acento es libre, es decir, recae en cualquier sílaba de la palabra' (minimal pairs kóɸe/koɸé, íʂati/iʂáti); statistically it tends to fall on the first syllable, secondarily the second, and more often on heavy syllables (V:, VC, CV:, CVV, CVC). Colombian Guainía Kurripako. Its Tabla 4 (p. 63, after Koch-Grünberg) equates 'Ipéka-Tapuyo' with 'Kumáta-Mínanei', Rio Aiary; Tabla 2 (Arahna) lists 'Ipéca, Alto Guainía' under Kurripako.
